blocks.text: 1. Multi-Tenancy
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448060783-844458167.png

Access Control closed by requiring a revoked permission to actually propagate, not remain a stale record. Multi-Tenancy, one RAG system serving multiple isolated customers or organizations, scales that same permission discipline up from individual users to entire separate organizations.
It keeps each tenant's data, cache, and queries completely separate within one shared infrastructure.
2. Multi-Tenancy Extends Access Control To Whole Organizations
Access Control covered separating what one user within an organization can see.
Multi-tenancy separates entire organizations from each other within the same running system.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Concept","What it separates"],"rows":[["Access control","What one user within an organization can see"],["Multi-tenancy","Entire separate organizations from each other"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Shared Infrastructure Versus Shared Visibility
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448060784-658672338.png
Running one shared vector database and pipeline does not mean any data is actually shared between tenants.
Infrastructure sharing and data visibility are two entirely separate concerns.
4. Tenant Identifiers Tagged On Absolutely Everything

blocks.alt: Tenant Identifiers Tagged On Absolutely Everything
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448060784-31918463.png
Every chunk, cache entry, and log record needs its owning tenant tagged on it, the same idea as the permission metadata attached to each chunk in Access Control.
A missing tenant tag is a direct path to leaking one tenant's data into another's results.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A chunk inserted without its tenant identifier risks surfacing in a different tenant's search results, the multi-tenant equivalent of the untagged-chunk risk covered in Access Control.

blocks.text: 5. Cross-Tenant Queries Must Never Leak
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448060784-500265256.png
A query from one tenant must never be able to retrieve another tenant's chunks, even accidentally, the same deny-by-default posture covered in Access Control.
Tenant isolation is treated as a hard boundary, not just a filtering preference.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Boundary type","How strictly it is enforced"],"rows":[["Regular permission filter","A preference applied during filtering"],["Tenant isolation","A hard boundary, never crossed under any condition"]]}

blocks.text: 6. Caching Across Multiple Tenants Needs Its Own Tenant-Scoped Keys

blocks.alt: Caching Across Multiple Tenants Needs Its Own Tenant-Scoped Keys
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448060973-962200462.png
A response cache key must include the tenant identifier, not just the query and context, extending the same idea that access control applies to cached results too in Access Control.
Without that, one tenant's cached answer could leak straight into another tenant's session.
7. Noisy Neighbors And Resource Contention
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448060973-585952625.png
One tenant's heavy usage can degrade latency for every other tenant sharing the same infrastructure, similar to the ongoing operational load that real-time updates add in Real-Time Updates.
Resource limits per tenant keep one heavy user from starving the rest.
8. Dedicated Infrastructure As An Alternative To Shared Multi-Tenancy
Some tenants require fully separate infrastructure rather than logical isolation within a shared system, an extension of securing infrastructure beyond the RAG pipeline itself in Security.
Full physical separation trades efficiency for the strongest possible isolation guarantee.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A tenant with strict regulatory requirements may require its own fully separate vector database and pipeline rather than relying on logical isolation within shared infrastructure, trading cost efficiency for a stronger guarantee.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Full Multi-Tenancy Support Is Worth Its Engineering Cost

blocks.alt: Recognizing When Full Multi-Tenancy Support Is Worth Its Engineering Cost
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448060973-211816232.png
A system serving multiple separate customers needs real multi-tenant isolation.
A system serving only one organization never needs tenant isolation at all.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming shared infrastructure automatically implies shared, safely visible data.
Forgetting to tag a chunk, cache entry, or log record with its owning tenant.
Building a response cache key without the tenant identifier, risking cross-tenant leakage.
Letting one tenant's heavy usage degrade latency for every other tenant with no resource limits.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Multi-tenancy lets one RAG system serve multiple isolated customers or organizations.
It extends access control from separating users within one organization to separating whole organizations.
Sharing infrastructure does not mean sharing data visibility; the two are separate concerns.
Every chunk, cache entry, and log record needs its owning tenant tagged on it.
Cross-tenant data access must be treated as a hard boundary, never crossed even accidentally.
A response cache key must include the tenant identifier to avoid leaking across tenants.
One tenant's heavy usage can degrade latency for others; per-tenant resource limits prevent this.
Some tenants require fully separate, dedicated infrastructure instead of logical isolation.
